items.title: A Mixed-Methods Study of Personal Software Creation
items.summary: People have long wanted software shaped around their own data, routines, and preferences. We refer to such software as \emph{personal software}. For decades, programming expertise limited who could build it: people without that expertise could build software only within constrained end-user programming tools, such as spreadsheets. AI coding agents seem to remove this bottleneck by letting people build full applications from natural-language descriptions, and many people now build and share personal software publicly. Yet personal software has rarely been studied at scale: we know little about what people build and why, how they build it, and what opportunities and challenges they encounter. We investigate these questions with a mixed-methods study. A grey-literature review examines 6,168 web and Reddit posts, and an observation study follows eight people as they build software for their own needs with AI coding agents and use it for up to a week. We find that creators value personal software for how closely it fits a particular person or community. The software takes shape as creators react to what the agent builds: most functionality emerged during building, and creators' effort shifted from writing code to checking it.

items.title: ACAP: Asynchronous Coding Agents for Efficient Robot Control
items.summary: Coding agents can construct and revise robot behavior during execution, but using one agent for the whole robot can delay otherwise independent work. We introduce Asynchronous Coding Agents as Policy (ACAP), an asynchronous framework that organizes one robot as a team of persistent agents. Each member reasons and acts for a configurable control group, such as an arm with its gripper or the torso and chassis, enabling asynchronous reasoning and execution. However, different robot components often have physical dependencies that require coordination. To address this challenge, ACAP introduces a hyper-agent that assigns tasks, coordinates dependencies, and dynamically allocates control between the lead and member agents. This allows independent work to progress concurrently while supporting tightly coupled manipulation when necessary. Across 72 real-world rollouts covering 25 task/platform settings, ACAP reduces task-balanced time cost by 28.2% compared with a single-agent Direct Policy, with improvements across Fully Parallel, Parallel-Sequential, and Collaborative tasks. Across all eight Collaborative settings, ACAP also achieves lower mean time cost than Fixed Delegation, where only member agents can control their assigned groups. An additional 90-rollout study shows lower mean 30-minute-capped time cost than Direct on all six tasks. We further demonstrate mobile manipulation using the same member interface for chassis and torso control. We present the framework and a real-world rollout dataset containing observations, generated programs, actions, and feedback to support research on how coding agents reason and act in the physical world.

items.title: AI-Assisted Auto-formalization for Trustworthy Scientific Computing: Case Studies and Lessons Learned
items.summary: Agentic AI tools have recently had success in mathematical reasoning. Both general purpose coding agents such as Claude Code and Codex, and specialized mathematics agents such as Aristotle, have been used for formalizing mathematical problems such as Fermat's last theorem, Erdős problems and several IMO level math problems. However, much of these efforts are concentrated in the pure mathematics domain, which benefits from relatively self-contained theorem statements, fixed mathematical representation and extensive support in existing formal libraries. Applied mathematics, on the other hand, presents additional challenges because the source may describe a computational procedure or modeling transformation rather than a declarative theorem. In this work, we present a systematic study of AI-assisted auto-formalization for scientific computing (SC), a domain in applied mathematics central to U.S. Department of Energy applications. Through case studies spanning hierarchical abstraction layers in SC software stack, we evaluate not only whether AI agents can complete numerical proofs, but also where and why they fail across the stack. Our primary contribution is a cross-layer taxonomy of failure modes and an analysis of the form of expert feedback required at each layer to recover mathematical soundness. From these observations, we derive a workflow for recurring proof patterns and practical guidance for using AI agents while preserving mathematical soundness. Our results characterize both the practical value and the current limitations of AI-assisted formalization for trustworthy scientific computing.

items.title: RoboUniverse-10K: Toward the Scaling Era of Agentic Robotics via Real-to-Sim Environments
items.summary: Agentic Robotics, in which foundation models act as coding agents to control robots through executable programs, has emerged as a compelling paradigm for embodied intelligence. Yet unlike software engineering, where massive executable environments power post-training, robotics remains constrained by small, manual benchmarks and in-distribution evaluation. To bridge this gap, we introduce RoboUniverse-10K, 10,807 interactive, resettable, and verifiable physics environments built from real-world videos via an automated Real2Sim and quality assurance pipeline. Each runs in an isolated, Harbor-compatible harness that hides privileged states and grading logic to mirror real-world sensing. From the same pipeline, we hold out 500 unseen tasks to establish RoboUniverse-Verified, an expert-verified zero-shot benchmark. Evaluating 11 closed- and open-source models reveals a huge gap: frontier models reach 85.8\% success, while open-source baselines lag at 2.6\% to 10.0\%, bottlenecked by low-level grasping, deformable-object manipulation, and post-contact physical control. Finally, we collect about 17K multi-turn trajectories totaling 0.79B tokens with GPT-6 Astra and perform full-parameter supervised fine-tuning on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, yielding RoboUniverse-35B-A3B. Our model achieves substantial zero-shot gains on RoboUniverse-Verified, lifting the success rate from 0.8\% to 21.2\%, while achieving zero-shot task completions across LIBERO-MAX, RoboCasa, RoboTwin 2.0, and a real Franka arm. We open-source the RL-ready environments and model to lay the foundation for large-scale reinforcement learning in Agentic Robotics.

items.title: Useful but Unwieldy: How Software Engineers Perceive the Design of Chain-of-Thought Explanations in Coding Agents
items.summary: Coding agents (CAs) powered by Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into software engineering (SE) workflows. As these CAs take up more tasks and responsibilities, it is imperative for software engineers to understand the CA's rationale behind its' decisions, also known as the chain-of-thought (CoT). During the interaction, some CAs are capable of showing this CoT as a separate message to users with the goal of providing transparency and explainability. However, its effectiveness as an explainable AI (XAI) mechanism for end-users in software engineering has not yet been established in the literature. This motivates us to understand their experiences with the CoT message as an XAI tool through a survey and semi-structured follow-up interviews with 36 software engineers. Through thematic analysis of the survey responses and interview transcripts, we found that CoT message is an indispensable tool for software engineers in terms of transparency, scrutability, and trust towards the CA. However, various instances of CoT messages being overly verbose, containing technical information that does not match the users' expertise, or being perceived by the users as ``detached'' from the conversation because the ``agent is talking to itself'', lead to comprehension difficulties and selective use or abandonment of the tool. We synthesize these insights to inform the design of CoT messages that support software engineers in their explainability needs.

items.title: Embo-Harness: Towards Understanding Frontier-Model-as-Policy Harness
items.summary: Frontier multimodal models exhibit extraordinary generalization in generating robot actions from observations and instructions, enabling a new paradigm in which they serve directly as policies within closed-loop robotic harnesses. However, the design principles of such harnesses, and the capabilities underlying their strong performance, remain unclear. We present Embo-Harness, a framework for systematically studying frontier-model-as-policy harnesses. We investigate four components of the robotic agentic loop, namely, prompting, planning, action execution, and tool use, and distill six empirical findings into a practical recipe. This recipe prioritizes interfaces that exploit the model's native visual reasoning and tool-use capabilities over handcrafted plans, skills, or action priors, and identifies effective choices for action representation, chunking, reasoning effort, visual observations, short multi-action sequences, and policy refinement. On RoboLab-120, Embo-Harness achieves an 83.3\% success rate, outperforming the strongest reported baseline by 26.2 percentage points. It also succeeds in 15 of 20 zero-shot trials across four real-world manipulation tasks. Beyond performance, controlled interventions indicate that the studied model depends more strongly on accurate spatial target estimation than on explicit low-level joint or trajectory generation. These results provide both a practical recipe for building strong frontier-model-as-policy harnesses and a clearer account of the capabilities that drive their performance.

items.title: Self-Upgrading Embodied Agents
items.summary: An embodied agent built on a language model goes to work with the weights it was given and keeps them for life. To get better, it needs more training, or reflection, memory, search or prompts that cost every step and are lost when the task changes. Editing weights by reasoning, weight-space programming, could end this, but has stayed with models that only reason or relied on a far larger commercial model. We introduce the self-upgrading embodied agent, to our knowledge the first that learns from its own experience by upgrading its own weights on the job, between its tasks, with no training, no gradient, no reward model, no second model, no test-time scaling and no harness or prompt engineering. By day a 27B agent works in a household environment. At night it reads its record, finds many of its steps wasted on replies that reach the token limit before any action, traces the habit to one direction in its hidden states, and rewrites one tensor of its weights. An agent that rewrites itself must first never break itself, so it is its own examiner: it tests every change against its unchanged self on practice tasks and keeps only what holds. When an edit holds, the next day it is a better agent, at the same cost per step: over thousands of held-out episodes, 48 fresh seeds a task, its one kept edit makes it complete significantly more tasks, in fewer steps, with fewer wasted and fewer tokens. This self-improvement is multi-round, stable and continual: through the nights that follow, the upgrade holds, without collapse. Of four sizes of its family, only the 27B agent does this. From here on, an embodied agent need not keep training and inference apart: as it works, it gathers its own experience and upgrades itself, with no separate pre-training or post-training and no human intervention. We believe this opens lifelong continual learning for robots: stable, continual, recursive self-improvement.

items.title: Preflight: Agentic Last-Mile Verification for AI Software Supply Chains
items.summary: Software dependencies execute within the trust boundary of downstream applications, yet provenance, static analysis, and package-level behavioral approaches do not directly determine how a released artifact behaves for a specific program. We present Preflight, a program-scoped pre-execution verifier for Python dependencies that extracts application-referenced symbols, iteratively synthesizes and validates function-level harnesses, executes resolved artifacts in a restricted environment, records behavioral fingerprints, and compares target behavior against prior versions when suitable baselines exist. We evaluate Preflight on four real software-supply-chain incidents under five application contexts, a 100-package benign corpus, and a controlled function-level versus import-only ablation. Preflight returns malicious verdicts in four incident contexts and a clean verdict in the LiteLLM client context, where the affected proxy-server path is not exercised. All 100 evaluated benign packages receive clean verdicts, with zero observed false positives. In a controlled ablation on Ultralytics and ctx, function-level harnesses expose malicious behavior in both incidents, whereas import-only probing exposes neither. Together, these results show that conditioning behavioral verification on the downstream program can expose security-relevant dependency behavior while remaining selective on benign workloads.

items.title: Real2Worlds2Real: Scaling Self-Improving Agentic Real2Sim2Real for Robot Manipulation
items.summary: Scaling robot manipulation learning remains challenging due to the high cost of collecting real-world interaction data. Real-to-Sim-to-Real (Real2Sim2Real) offers a promising route by enabling policy learning in simulation grounded in real-world observations, yet scaling this paradigm across diverse tasks and physical interactions remains difficult. We introduce Real2Worlds2Real, a self-improving agentic framework that integrates scalable simulation-world construction with policy development. Given limited visual observations and task descriptions, its tool-orchestration harness constructs faithful digital twins and expands them into diverse, physically executable digital cousins. The agent adaptively selects tools and revisits construction decisions, using visual and execution feedback to refine geometry and physical behavior. Building on these worlds, the agent orchestrates policy development by coordinating data generation, policy learning, and refinement based on task requirements and simulation rollout feedback. Across both stages, the agent distills validated procedures into reusable skills that guide subsequent tasks. Experiments demonstrate improved world fidelity and successful real-world policy transfer, with performance gains from increasing world diversity and interaction-data volume. Skill reuse further improves world-building efficiency and long-horizon task success.

items.title: ReWeave: Emergent Physical Task Topologies for Embodied Harness Optimization and Cross-Task Meta-Distillation
items.summary: Long-horizon embodied tasks involve physical dependencies that may only become clear through interaction. As task understanding deepens, past trials can reveal new information for adaptation and transfer. However, coarse progress feedback cannot identify which physical preconditions held, leaving search unguided, while task-specific optimization easily overfits to individual scenes, making cross-task transfer brittle. We introduce ReWeave, a framework that jointly optimizes an embodied agent harness and an emergent physical task topology from interaction without updating policy weights. Keeping execution policies and perception frozen, ReWeave co-optimizes coupled context, workflows, and control loops. As new evidence revises the topology, ReWeave reprojects past trials onto the updated task understanding, exposing retained progress, regressions, and bottlenecks that guide parent selection and search width. Across tasks, matching verified local mechanisms to unmet preconditions consolidates 72 specialist units into 44 reusable groups ($0.34\times$ full concatenation) within a compact shared harness capable of continual learning. ReWeave improves held-out success from 89.00% to 98.75% on LIBERO-PRO and from 25.50% to 58.25% on RoboDojo, while uncovering retained progress in 89% of 159 failed RoboDojo development trials and translating stronger offline reasoning into higher online performance. On eight unseen LIBERO-PRO tasks, the shared harness reaches 51.3% success versus 41.3% for direct distillation, rising to 75.0% after continual learning.

items.title: CompAct-Bench: A Benchmark for Working-Context Compaction in Long-Horizon Agent Tasks
items.summary: As language-model agents are applied to increasingly extended tasks, their working context continuously accumulates interaction history, tool observations, intermediate decisions, and task progress. Context compaction offers a practical way to reduce this growing history while allowing execution to continue, yet the compaction ability of modern LLMs remains insufficiently understood. We introduce CompAct-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating working-context compaction through its downstream effect on agent task completion. Starting from successful agent trajectories, we insert compaction boundaries at different stages of execution, compress the preceding working context with the model under evaluation, and let the same executor continue the original task. To enable fair comparison across compactors, we evaluate them under controlled retention ratios using a lightweight iterative ratio-adjustment procedure. CompAct-Bench covers information-seeking, software-engineering, and workspace-oriented tasks through BrowseComp, SWE-bench, and an internal CompanyBench evaluation. Our experiments show that working-context compaction remains highly lossy even for frontier models: Claude- and GPT-family models perform strongest overall, yet substantial degradation in downstream task accuracy persists under aggressive compaction. Further analysis reveals that failures are often caused not only by omitted information, but also by distorted task state, such as turning unresolved issues into apparent conclusions or forgetting previously established results, which can lead to incorrect decisions or redundant execution. These findings highlight working-context compaction as a distinct and still challenging ability for LLMs operating in extended agent tasks.

items.title: Securing and Auditing Long-Horizon LLM Agents: State-Transfer Auditing and Controls in the Agent Harness
items.summary: Long-horizon LLM agents across codebases, web browsers, and enterprise infrastructure rely on an execution harness to move state between the working context, session history, persistent memory, and external environment. While conventional execution traces log model prompts and tool calls, critical security and reliability failures occur during state transfers: a transfer can admit unchecked content (indirect prompt injections, unverified memory writes), rewrite state lossily (context compaction dropping user constraints, memory consolidation stripping source authority), or restore state incompletely (workspace rollbacks leaving aborted KV state active on the inference server). Because current traces omit what crosses these boundaries, failure attribution and runtime monitors fail on multi-step trajectories. We present a state-transfer audit architecture for the agent harness. At each transfer boundary, we define an audit point specifying the minimal hash-chained record the harness emits, separating low-overhead deterministic checks from model-based semantic checks and binding internal context, memory, and inference-server cache state to external actions. We show that the same transfer records required for causal failure attribution supply the durable state needed by runtime security controls, including least-privilege capabilities, replay-resistant authorization outside the prompt, information flow control, obligation monitors, and transactional recovery across multi-agent and infrastructure pipelines. Finally, we analyze multimodal GUI adaptations and implement and evaluate a reference harness middleware across 240 multi-step fault-injection trajectories, showing that transfer records localize root causes and catch cross-transfer violations missed by lifecycle and tool-only logs at microsecond deterministic overhead.

items.title: SpecCompact: Accelerating LLM Agent Context Compaction with Slot-Parallel Semantic Speculative Verification
items.summary: LLM agents use context compaction to manage growing interaction histories, but summarizing long histories with large models can introduce substantial delays. Compaction therefore requires balancing information retention against latency. We observe that structured summary slots can retain information when generated independently. Based on this observation, we present SpecCompact, a framework that accelerates compaction through slot-parallel semantic speculation. SpecCompact fine-tunes a small drafter and generates slots in parallel. The target model verifies each proposed line and repairs rejected content, while subsequent drafting uses the updated slot prefix. System optimizations further reduce repeated context processing and model calls. Across AppWorld and $τ^3$ benchmarks with two target models, SpecCompact achieves $2.04$--$5.63\times$ compaction speedups over Hermes-style summarization. Separate downstream evaluations reveal model- and task-dependent performance trade-offs. A user study within Hermes further shows an $8.68\times$ median compaction speedup.

items.title: SUMONE: A Simple and Efficient Summarizer for Plug-and-Play Agent Memory
items.summary: Long-horizon language-model agents accumulate increasingly large interaction histories, making context compaction essential for efficient execution. Existing learned compaction methods often rely on downstream task outcomes or solver behavior, coupling training to specific tasks or agents. We introduce SumOne, a standalone summarizer trained to preserve information in agent histories through masked reconstruction. Given a summary of the expired history, a frozen reconstructor recovers randomly masked portions of the original trajectory; reconstruction quality, combined with a length penalty, provides a task-agnostic reward for optimizing the summarizer with GRPO. This yields self-supervision directly from raw trajectories, without reference summaries or downstream task execution. At inference time, only the lightweight summarizer is retained, enabling plug-and-play context compression for otherwise unchanged agents. We conduct a systematic evaluation of SumOne in long-horizon search and software-engineering tasks. SumOne reduces estimated inference cost by approximately 78\% on DeepSearchQA and 75\% on SWE-bench Verified relative to operating with full context, with absolute decreases of 0.04. The same checkpoint also transfers across downstream models and agent harnesses without additional fine-tuning.

items.title: Fast, Cheap, and Fair? Evaluating Decision Models
items.summary: Industries are increasingly adopting AI-driven systems to automate a wide range of tasks, including high-stakes decisions in human resources, such as candidate screening and recruitment. This makes evaluating their fairness essential, particularly when decisions directly affect individuals' opportunities. Accordingly, the EU AI Act classifies recruitment AI systems as high-risk, imposing strict requirements on their deployment. In this context, compact ``System~1'' decision models offer a fast and cost-efficient alternative to general-purpose LLMs, yet their fairness remains largely unexplored. This article presents the first systematic bias and fairness audit of \jev{}, a typed-decision model targeting recruitment applications. The study evaluates how explicit demographic attributes and implicit candidate cues influence screening scores, rankings, and shortlisting outcomes. These effects are compared against a noise floor derived from name substitutions and typographical variations. The evaluation also examines output validity, latency, and cost. Counterfactual CV datasets and evaluation code are released for reproducibility.

items.title: MedUIGym: Evaluating and Training GUI Agents for Clinical Workflows
items.summary: Automating clinical workflows requires vision-language agents that can navigate dense graphical user interfaces (GUIs) in electronic health records (EHRs) and execute precise actions, yet many medical agents still rely on text or structured tool calls. In this work, we introduce MedUIGym, a scalable interactive environment comprising 15,739 tasks from 17 benchmark sources across six clinical task families for training and evaluating clinical GUI agents. In MedUIGym, agents perceive EHR states from screenshots and execute mouse-and-keyboard actions, as well as a paired native-tool interface over identical clinical data. The environment verifies both final answers and required clinical actions, and supports parallel trajectory collection for training. Benchmarking twelve vision-language models shows that current agents struggle across diverse clinical workflows, and simply increasing reasoning effort fails to yield consistent gains. Furthermore, MedUIGym supports offline learning from GUI trajectories and online reinforcement learning from task rewards. After training, both Qwen3.5 models perform better on in-domain clinical tasks and generalize to tasks from external sources. By unifying tasks from existing benchmarks, dual-interface evaluation, and GUI trajectory collection, MedUIGym provides a testbed for studying how vision-language agents complete clinical tasks through the EHR's graphical interface. Our project page is available at https://github.com/yitong-qiao/MedUIGym.

items.title: Can Cities Have Personalities? Introducing the SCD City Personality Assessment
items.summary: Descriptions of cities are shaped by human experience and institutional narratives. We introduce the SCD City Personality Assessment (SCD-CPA), a method that instantiates document-grounded ChatGPT city personas and interrogates each with an identical 24-statement instrument inspired by the four-pair structure of the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator. Rather than asking a general-purpose model to characterize cities freely, we configure a separate document-grounded conversational agent for each city and use alternative evidence portraits to compare documentary inputs. The resulting four bipolar dimensions and four-letter summaries use independently defined urban concepts and scoring rules. Tokyo, New York, and Paris form the methodological evaluation (33 assessments across repeated sessions, three GPT-6 effort settings, and alternative portraits): Tokyo's original portrait yielded 85.4% exact within-setting item agreement, while evidence substitutions shifted some dimension strengths. A five-city application to Shanghai, Dubai, Mumbai, Lagos, and Sao Paulo (15 assessments) yielded 77.8% exact and 99.4% within-one-point cross-setting agreement, indicating consistency under the tested configurations. By treating each city conversational agent as a reproducible, evidence-conditioned experimental configuration, SCD-CPA makes documented city-character perceptions comparable and exposes their sensitivity to source selection. Although the documentary evidence is explicitly controlled, the model's internal interpretation of that evidence cannot be fully observed. We also examine the robustness of SCD-CPA across three AI reasoning-effort settings. The observed consistency suggests that the methodology is relatively insensitive to the tested configuration differences and provides a framework for evaluating its stability as future generations of AI models become available.

items.title: Can Vibe Coding Produce Accessible Websites: An Empirical Study on LLM Coding Agents and Skills
items.summary: Large language model (LLM) coding agents increasingly allow developers and non-professionals to create websites through natural-language instructions, with limited inspection of the generated source code. Although this ``vibe coding'' workflow lowers barriers to software creation, it may also propagate accessibility defects at scale. We investigate the accessibility of websites generated end-to-end by contemporary coding agents and whether agent-level accessibility interventions improve their output. We generated 90 websites for three projects using combinations of three coding agents, four language models, and multiple reasoning-effort levels. We evaluated complete interaction journeys using axe-core, IBM Equal Access Accessibility Checker, and QualWeb, and converged reports to observe violation prevalence and violated WCAG Success Criterion (SC). None of the 90 baseline websites was fully accessible, with an average of 80.43 violated interface elements. 13 WCAG SCs were violated at least once across the runs. Color contrast was the most prevalent issue, followed by labeling, semantic-structure, keyboard, and visualization failures. We reran 24 matched configurations with a general accessibility Skill and a contrast-specific Skill. Both significantly improved accessibility scores, but neither eliminated violations. User testing with blind individuals corroborated the experiential effects of the detected inaccessibilities. Moreover, functional correctness decreased with the inclusion of Skills. Our findings show that accessibility does not reliably emerge from vibe coding, and agentic interventions can both improve some accessibility issues and introduce new functional ones.

items.title: Autonomous Parameter Surgery: How LLMs Implant Selective Backdoors into Language Models
items.summary: Neural network weights are usually treated as opaque artifacts of gradient descent. Recent work on weight space programming, however, suggests that large language models can inspect and rewrite another network's parameters directly. In this paper, we ask whether a general language model can turn a natural language backdoor specification into persistent, selective weight edits on its own, without gradient training, layer hints, external corpora, or a prescribed editing formula. Using DeepSeek Flash at low reasoning effort inside a restricted workspace that blocks local CPU simulation, we test three open models (Qwen3.5-0.8B, Llama-3.2-1B, SmolLM3-3B) across two review domains (IMDb and Yelp; 18 independent sessions). Evaluated in fresh processes with the editor removed, the modified checkpoints reach 99.2% mean attack success on the editing domain and 97.6% transfer success on the unseen domain, while preserving clean accuracy, low control drift, and general capabilities within 1.7 points of the base models. Our traces show that the model converges on edits in the final layer in 17 of 18 runs and discovers both dense rank-one orthogonalization and single neuron weight surgery at an average cost of \$1.74 per run.
